scenes.title: Auto Scaling processes: nine independent controls

scenes.narration: This slide is a reference map of nine Auto Scaling processes, each responsible for a different operation. Read the grid left to right. Across the top, Launch creates instances, Terminate removes them, and HealthCheck evaluates supported health sources and marks unhealthy instances. The next row contains ReplaceUnhealthy, which acts on unhealthy capacity; AZRebalance, which adjusts capacity distribution across configured Availability Zones; and AlarmNotification, which processes CloudWatch alarm-driven scaling activity. On the bottom row, ScheduledActions applies configured scheduled capacity changes, AddToLoadBalancer registers new instances with the configured load balancer or target group, and InstanceRefresh replaces instances during an initiated refresh. These names are specific controls, not nine sequential steps every launch performs. Notice the reminder strip: suspending one process does not suspend the entire Auto Scaling group. For example, an instance may be created but fail to register if the load-balancer registration process is suspended. When investigating unexpected behavior, identify the precise suspended process and its side effects, then plan how to resume safely. Do not disable broad Auto Scaling behavior simply to silence an alarm.

scenes.title: Suspended processes: diagnose unexpected side effects
scenes.visual_overview: Four warning panels illustrate suspended Launch, ReplaceUnhealthy, AddToLoadBalancer and ScheduledActions with bottom checks before resumption and Spot caveat.
visual_walkthrough: Explain Launch suspended: scale-out cannot create replacements even if other processes terminate instances
Explain ReplaceUnhealthy suspended: unhealthy instances may be marked but replacement waits
Trace AddToLoadBalancer suspended: launched instances are not automatically registered after resumption
Explain ScheduledActions suspended: missed schedules are not replayed
Use bottom checklist to check capacity, health, registrations and Spot interruption risks before resuming

scenes.narration: The purpose of this slide is to show that suspending Auto Scaling processes can create surprising combinations. Begin with the upper-left warning. When Launch is suspended, a scale-out demand cannot create new instances. If ReplaceUnhealthy remains active, unhealthy instances may still be terminated without replacements arriving, reducing capacity further. The upper-right panel covers the opposite side: ReplaceUnhealthy is suspended, but health checking can still identify unhealthy instances. Automated replacement then waits until that process resumes. Now inspect the lower-left blue panel, AddToLoadBalancer. New instances can launch without being registered with the load balancer, and resuming the process does not automatically register the instances that were missed. Explicitly check registration. In the purple lower-right panel, ScheduledActions misses scheduled changes while suspended, and resuming does not replay those missed actions. The final checklist asks the operator to inspect desired versus healthy capacity, pending replacements, target registration and configuration before restoring processes. The yellow warning is another boundary: suspending Terminate does not prevent the Spot service from interrupting a Spot instance. The SAP takeaway is to understand each process's effect and repair state deliberately, rather than assuming resume catches everything up.

Distinguish restoring previous traffic from reversing data or state changes

scenes.narration: This final slide compares three deployment patterns rather than one workflow. On the left, a rolling instance refresh replaces instances inside a single Auto Scaling group using a new launch-template version. Healthy-capacity percentages, warmup, alarms and checkpoints help constrain rollout risk, but you still need enough usable capacity. In the center, two parallel Auto Scaling groups serve v1 and v2. They can use separate target groups behind one Application Load Balancer, allowing weighted forwarding toward the new version while monitoring its behavior. This is useful when keeping the previous fleet available is important. On the right, each fleet has a separate load balancer and Route 53 weighted records influence which endpoint clients resolve. Unlike ALB target-group weighting, DNS selection is subject to recursive and client caching, so cutover is not instantaneous. The lower panel says to preserve isolated test access, validate long-lived sessions, plan spare capacity and ensure application-to-database compatibility before switching. The reminder closes the real rollback constraint. Sending traffic back to v1 does not undo schema migrations, reverse writes or recover lost application state. Select the rollout architecture that matches blast radius, recovery needs and data compatibility.
